title: Keep yourselves in the love of God (Jude 20–25)
hookLine: Jude ends with a glorious blessing to him who can keep you from falling

lines: A SINGLE PAGE, EASY TO SKIP.
cards: Some letters are easy to skip.
The letter of Jude is a single page, tucked in just before the last book of the Bible, and most of it is a fierce warning about false teachers, with strange references to angels and old stories.
People flip past it on their way to the Apocalypse. But before signing off, the writer ends with a blessing that still gets prayed today, and it's the last stop on this long road through the letters.

teach.b: Jude introduces himself as the servant of Jesus Christ and the brother of James. Catholic tradition has long identified him with the apostle Jude, also called Thaddeus, whom it honors as a patron of desperate causes.
Scholars discuss who exactly he was. Near the end, he turns from the danger to his readers, and gives them three things to do. Build yourselves up on your faith.

teach.h: KEEP YOURSELVES IN THE LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: And, in the Douay-Rheims: "Keep yourselves in the love of God." It's a picture of staying put, inside a love that is already there, the way you stay near a fire on a cold night.
Then he adds: be merciful to those who doubt, and pull others out of the fire. And then, the blessing.

In the Douay-Rheims it begins: "Now to him who is able to preserve you without sin, and to present you spotless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy." The King James puts it as keep you from falling.
Look at the shape of that. Jude has just told his readers to keep themselves in God's love.

teach.h: HIM WHO IS ABLE TO KEEP YOU.
teach.b: Then he gives the glory to the one who is able to keep them. Both are true at once.
A blessing like this, one that ends a letter by giving glory to God, has a name: doxology, from the Greek doxa, glory, and logos, word.

teach.h: TO HIM WHO IS ABLE TO PRESERVE YOU.

teach.b: Catholics pray doxologies often: the Glory Be at the end of each decade of the rosary, and at Mass, the great one at the end of the Eucharistic Prayer, when the priest lifts the host and chalice and the people answer, Amen.

how: Catholics pray doxologies many times a day: the Glory Be after psalms and at each decade of the rosary, and at Mass the great doxology that ends the Eucharistic Prayer, to which the people answer Amen; Saint Jude is also invoked in desperate situations.

a word of glory, giving praise to God

he ends with a blessing: to him who is able to preserve you without sin.

games.q: you're Jude. you've just written a page of hard warnings about false teachers. how do you end the letter?
o: with a blessing giving glory to God, who is able to keep them.
with a list of names to avoid.
games.why: Jude ends with a doxology: to him who is able to preserve you without sin, and present you spotless with exceeding joy.

practice: Bring to mind someone who seems close to falling: a friend struggling with faith, a teenager, someone tired of trying.

If you pray, say the start of Jude's blessing slowly for them, now to him who is able to preserve you without sin, and give the glory where Jude gives it. If you don't pray, hold them in mind and wish them steady footing.

wordCard.voice: Doxology. A word of glory to God, like the blessing that ends Jude's letter. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: glory, the first half of doxology; Jude 25 gives glory to the only God our Savior.

carryVoice: Your line: able to keep you. And that's the letters, from Romans to Jude. Tomorrow, the last book.
